first.rationale: Simplifying onboarding directly addresses the current completion decline and is supported by prior evidence of improved completion, time-to-value, early adoption, and SMB activation. Promotional pricing is worth verifying because of the competitor threat, but its known 30-day retention downside makes it a weaker candidate for sustainable qualified revenue unless the source record materially narrows that risk.

mid.rationale: Run a standard experiment simplifying onboarding. It directly addresses the 4% decline in completion and has confirmed prior effects on completion (+13%), time-to-value (-2.1 days), and 30-day retention (+3%), while related signup simplification also durably improved SMB first-week activation. This is the strongest sustainable-revenue response available this cycle. Do not use promotional pricing: its acquisition and qualified-revenue gains were paired with a 12% 30-day retention decline and failure to survive the first renewal cycle.

final2.rationale: Keep the onboarding-simplification experiment. It is the only candidate with confirmed improvement in completion, time-to-value, and 30-day retention, and it directly addresses the current completion and activation declines. The deeper competitor cut increases urgency, but does not overturn the evidence that targeted promotional pricing acquires a cohort that fails to survive renewal and reduces 30-day retention by 12%; using it would sacrifice sustainable qualified revenue for a short-term response. Monitor SMB churn conversations and competitor impact, but do not replace the committed experiment with discounting without new evidence.
